messages.subject: Advice on discrete parameter conversion
parts:
Hi, I'm new to stan and bayesian inference, so I thought that stan will lessen my stress on building MCMC sampler.
Only after noticing that stan does not allow int parameter sampling, I am confused on how to solve the problem.
I saw on the reference and other threads that general solution is to marginalize out the discrete parameter by specifying full posterior. My question is do I have to decompose full posterior to marginalize out the parameter or working with conditional posterior is sufficient.
The following is part of model, excluding other predictors, somewhat naively coded in stan. I thought of building bionial logit with explicit group and implicit group. For implicit group, HMM (2 state in this case) is used to control the varying intercept; but you see there is conditionally beta bernoulli, so we can write out analytic conditional posterior for that term. Any advice would be appreciated including flaws in code.
Thanks, SB.

data {
  int<lower=1> N;        // Number of total obs in long format Data 
  int<lower=1> I;        // Number of people
  int<lower=1> T;        // Number of Years
  int<lower=1, upper=N> ii_u[I]; // people starting idx
  int<lower=0> PARENT[N];
  int<lower=0> LEFT[N];
  int<lower=1> N_g;   // Number of Exgroup
  row_vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N_g] X_g[N]; // Design matrix wrt Exgroup
}
parameters {
  ordered [2] alphas; // Hidden group effect
  simplex [2] nu[2];  // Transition probs
  int<lower=0, upper=1> Eit[N]; // Hidden group indicator
  vector [N_g] bet; // Exgroup Effect
  
  for(i in 1:I)
    Eit[ii_u[i]] = 0;  // initialize first mon group to 0
}
model {
  vector[N] Reg;
  alphas ~ normal(0, 5);
  bet ~ normal(0, 5);
 
  for (s in 1:2)
    nu[s] ~ beta(1,1);
 
  // HMM on Hidden group
  for (i in 2:N) {
    for (t in (ii_u[i-1]+1):ii_u[i]) {
      Eit[t] ~ bernoulli(nu[Eit[t-1]]);
    }
  }
  // Update alpha
  alpha = Eit * alphas[1] + (1 - Eit) * alphas[2]
  for (n in 1:N)
    Reg[n] = alpha + (X_group[n] * bet);
  LEFT ~ binomial_logit(PARENT, Reg);
}

parts:
> On Aug 2, 2016, at 12:10 AM, SB Lee <sblee...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Hi, I'm new to stan and bayesian inference, so I thought that stan will lessen my stress on building MCMC sampler.

With Stan, you don't need to build an MCMC sampler, it's
already built in.

> Only after noticing that stan does not allow int parameter sampling, I am confused on how to solve the problem.
> I saw on the reference and other threads that general solution is to marginalize out the discrete parameter by specifying full posterior. My question is do I have to decompose full posterior to marginalize out the parameter or working with conditional posterior is sufficient.

If you have posterior p(alpha, beta) where beta are the
integer parameters, you need to code up the marginalization

p(alpha) = SUM_beta p(alpha, beta)

Usually algebra lets you move that summation inside to make
it tractable. Often this would be of the form

PROD_k p(alpha[k] | beta[k]) * p(beta[k]).

if that's what you mean.

> The following is part of model, excluding other predictors, somewhat naively coded in stan. I thought of building bionial logit with explicit group and implicit group. For implicit group, HMM (2 state in this case) is used to control the varying intercept; but you see there is conditionally beta bernoulli, so we can write out analytic conditional posterior for that term. Any advice would be appreciated including flaws in code.
> Thanks, SB.
>
> data {
> int<lower=1> N; // Number of total obs in long format Data
> int<lower=1> I; // Number of people
> int<lower=1> T; // Number of Years
> int<lower=1, upper=N> ii_u[I]; // people starting idx
> int<lower=0> PARENT[N];
> int<lower=0> LEFT[N];
> int<lower=1> N_g; // Number of Exgroup
> row_vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N_g] X_g[N]; // Design matrix wrt Exgroup
> }
> parameters {
> ordered [2] alphas; // Hidden group effect
> simplex [2] nu[2]; // Transition probs
> int<lower=0, upper=1> Eit[N]; // Hidden group indicator
> vector [N_g] bet; // Exgroup Effect
>
> for(i in 1:I)
> Eit[ii_u[i]] = 0; // initialize first mon group to 0

You can't put statements in parameters block. It helps if
you send us Stna programs that compile. Did uou mean to
make this a transformed parameter? Also, this won't
set all elements of Eit to 0 depending on the value of ii_u.
Instead, you just want to do

E_it = rep_array(0, N);

> }
> model {
> vector[N] Reg;
> alphas ~ normal(0, 5);
> bet ~ normal(0, 5);
>
> for (s in 1:2)
> nu[s] ~ beta(1,1);

You don't need this as beta(1, 1) isuniform and
that's the default. Also, it doesn't make sense to
independently put priors on the members of a simplex.
The Dirichlet is the right generalization of the beta,
but you don't even need that here.

> // HMM on Hidden group
> for (i in 2:N) {
> for (t in (ii_u[i-1]+1):ii_u[i]) {
> Eit[t] ~ bernoulli(nu[Eit[t-1]]);
> }
> }

I can't follow your inteniton here. This isn't
the usual form of an HMM.

> // Update alpha
> alpha = Eit * alphas[1] + (1 - Eit) * alphas[2]
> for (n in 1:N)
> Reg[n] = alpha + (X_group[n] * bet);

You can vectorize this as

Reg = alpha + X_group * bet;

And I'd suggest spelling out "beta" if that was the intent.

> LEFT ~ binomial_logit(PARENT, Reg);

Also, we like to reserve all caps variables for constants.

- Bob

parts:
Thanks for the reply, Bob. I think I didn't clearly state the intention of the model.
1. The data is constructed in Sparse Data Structure just as in reference 13.1, ordered by person and mon respectively. 
2. Marginializing would required for parameter Eit in my case, which should be eliminated in my code. This is making me headache.
3. My fault. The first loop in HMM should have been 'for (i in 2:I)'. The intention was that the hidden group (2 states - 0 for baseline state and 1 for excited state - with transition probability nu s) make markov transitions wrt mon for each person. To be specific, for each person i, E_{i,(t+1)} ~ categorical(nu_{E_it, 0}, nu_{E_it, 1}) where E is binary.
So, setting Eit[ii_u[i]] = 0 means setting initial state as 0 for all people for their first month.
After E_{i,(t+1)} is determined, alpha = Eit * alphas[1] + (1 - Eit) * alphas[2] with alphas[1] < alphas[2] in generative sense.

I didn't see a question in there.

For 3, categorical distributions only have a single parameter,
the simplex of possible outcomes. But if there are only two,
it is a bit more efficient to use a beta-Bernoulli model than
a Dirichlet-categorical.

If you want to marginalize out the latent states in an HMM,
the manual shows how to use the forward algorithm to do that
in the HMM example in section 7.6.

- Bob

parts:
It doesn't matter what the output model is. If you
observe the discrete outputs, you estimate a multinomial,
if you observe continous outputs and have predictors, you
can estimate a linear model.
